title: Neptunus. Portus Libycus
titleEn: Neptune Stills the Storm — Aeneid I.102–197
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The storm Juno ordered breaks over the Trojan fleet: oars snap, ships are flung on reefs and sandbanks, one goes down before Aeneas's eyes. Then Neptune, lord of the sea, feels his realm in uproar, rebukes the winds for trespassing on it, and calms the waves — and Virgil gives his first full-scale simile, comparing the god to a statesman who quiets a rioting crowd with a word. Seven ships limp into a sheltered harbour on the Libyan coast; Achates lights a fire, Aeneas climbs a crag to look for the missing ships, finds none, and shoots seven stags, one for each crew. As in the first part, Virgil is rewriting the Odyssey: the storm, the harbour with its cave of the nymphs and the hunt on a strange shore are all Homer's, retold for Rome.

sentences.t:
Talia iactanti stridens Aquilone procella
velum adversa ferit, fluctusque ad sidera tollit.
sentences.l:
To him hurling such words, a gale, screeching with the North Wind,
strikes the sail head-on, and lifts the waves to the stars.
sentences.i: Even as he cries out so, a squall howling out of the north hits the sail head-on and flings the waves up to the stars.
sentences.n: 'iactanti' — dative, 'to him (Aeneas) flinging out such words', the person affected by what happens; 'talia' picks up his outcry of lines 94–101, so the storm answers him as he speaks. 'Aquilone' — the North Wind, ablative ('with, from'). 'adversa' agrees with 'procella': the gust comes from dead ahead. 'ad sidera' — to the stars, epic exaggeration. The whole storm is rebuilt from Odysseus' storm in Odyssey 5, where a great wave falls on him just as he finishes wishing he had died at Troy — the order Virgil keeps here.

sentences.t: Franguntur remi;
sentences.l: The oars are shattered;
sentences.i: The oars snap;
sentences.n: Verb first, clause short: from here to line 107 the damage comes in a run of quick blows, a clause for each. 'Franguntur' — 'are broken', present tense, the vivid narrative present that carries most of the storm.

sentences.t:
tum prora avertit, et undis
dat latus;
sentences.l:
then the prow turns away, and to the waves
gives its side;
sentences.i: then the bow slews round and turns the ship's flank to the waves;
sentences.n: 'avertit' is used without an object here, 'turns away'. With the bow knocked off course the ship lies broadside to the seas, the most dangerous position a ship can be in. 'undis' — dative, 'to the waves'.

sentences.t: insequitur cumulo praeruptus aquae mons.
sentences.l: there follows, piled up, a steep mountain of water.
sentences.i: and close behind comes a mountain of water, heaped up steep.
sentences.n: 'cumulo' — 'in a heap', ablative of manner. The line ends on a single-syllable word, 'mons', which Virgil rarely allows at the close of a hexameter: the rhythm breaks as the wave breaks. 'aquae mons' — 'a mountain of water', a picture from the Odyssey's storms.

sentences.t: Hi summo in fluctu pendent;
sentences.l: These on the topmost wave hang;
sentences.i: Some crews are left hanging at the top of a wave;
sentences.n: 'Hi… his' — 'these… to those': the crews of different ships, some lifted high and some dropped low. 'summo in fluctu' — 'on the top of the wave': 'summus' often means 'the top part of' something rather than 'highest'.

sentences.t:
his unda dehiscens
terram inter fluctus aperit;
sentences.l:
to those the wave, gaping,
the earth between the waves lays open;
sentences.i: for others the water gapes and bares the sea-floor between the waves;
sentences.n: 'his' — dative, 'for these'. 'dehiscens' — splitting open. 'terram' is the sea-bed itself, glimpsed at the bottom of the trough. 'inter fluctus' — between the walls of water on either side.

sentences.t: furit aestus harenis.
sentences.l: the surge rages with sand.
sentences.i: the tide boils thick with sand.
sentences.n: 'harenis' — 'with sands', ablative: the churned water is thick with sand torn from the bottom. Greenough spells 'harena' with h, the older form; 'arena' is also found. The plural of a mass noun ('sands') is common in verse.

sentences.i: The South Wind snatches three ships and spins them onto lurking rocks — rocks out in mid-sea that the Italians name the Altars — a vast spine lying at the surface;
sentences.n: 'Tris' = 'tres' (with 'navis' understood), Greenough's -is accusative plural, the old ending of i-stem words (you'll see this constantly: 'navis', 'omnis', 'Syrtis'). 'Notus' is the South Wind; 'Eurus', in line 110, the East. Between the dashes is a learned aside, with the relative 'quae' placed late and its antecedent 'saxa' pulled to the front: 'rocks which the Italians call Altars'. Virgil speaks here as a Roman of his own day. The Altars were reefs in the open sea somewhere between Sicily and Africa; Virgil says no more. 'dorsum' — a back, a ridge: the reef shows like the back of a sea-beast. 'mari summo' — at the top of the sea, just at the surface.

sentences.t:
tris Eurus ab alto
in brevia et Syrtis urguet, miserabile visu,
inliditque vadis atque aggere cingit harenae.
sentences.l:
three the East Wind from the deep
into the shallows and the Syrtes drives, pitiful to see,
and dashes them on the shoals, and encircles them with a rampart of sand.
sentences.i: the East Wind forces three more out of deep water onto the shallows and the Syrtes — a pitiful sight — smashes them on the shoals and rings them with a rampart of sand.
sentences.n: 'ab alto' — 'from the deep', the open sea ('altum' as a noun, which you'll meet often). 'brevia' — 'short places', shallows, a neuter adjective used as a noun. The Syrtes are two great gulfs of shifting sandbanks off the coast of Libya, notorious to ancient sailors; 'Syrtis' is again the -is accusative plural. 'urguet' is Greenough's spelling of 'urget' (The Latin Library prints 'urget': the same word). 'miserabile visu' — 'pitiful to see': 'visu' is the supine in -u, 'in the seeing', used with an adjective. 'aggere harenae' — 'with a rampart of sand': the stranded ships are as good as besieged.

sentences.t:
Unam, quae Lycios fidumque vehebat Oronten,
ipsius ante oculos ingens a vertice pontus
in puppim ferit:
sentences.l:
One, which carried the Lycians and loyal Orontes,
before the man's own eyes a huge sea from on high
strikes upon the stern:
sentences.i: One ship, which carried the Lycians and loyal Orontes, takes a monstrous sea from overhead full on the stern, before Aeneas's own eyes:
sentences.n: 'Unam' (navem) stands first as the object, and its subject, 'pontus', does not arrive until the end of the next line: the reader waits, as the ship does, for the blow. 'ipsius' — 'of the man himself', Aeneas, who watches helpless. The Lycians, from south-west Asia Minor, fought for Troy in the Iliad under Sarpedon. 'Oronten' is a Greek accusative (Orontes); Greek names in Virgil often keep their Greek endings. 'a vertice' — 'from the top', from overhead. 'pontus' — the sea (a Greek word), here a single towering wave.

sentences.t:
excutitur pronusque magister
volvitur in caput;
sentences.l:
is shaken out, and headlong the helmsman
is rolled onto his head;
sentences.i: the helmsman is flung out and pitched headfirst into the sea;
sentences.n: 'excutitur' — 'is shaken out', thrown from the ship. 'magister' here is the helmsman, the master of the ship, not a teacher. 'volvitur in caput' — 'is rolled onto his head', tumbling headfirst. A helmsman lost overboard recalls Odyssey 12, where Odysseus' helmsman is struck down when Zeus wrecks the ship; Aeneas will lose another, Palinurus, at the end of Book 5.

sentences.t:
ast illam ter fluctus ibidem
torquet agens circum, et rapidus vorat aequore vortex.
sentences.l:
but her three times the wave, in that same spot,
whirls, driving her round, and the racing whirlpool swallows her in the sea.
sentences.i: while the ship herself is spun three times round on the spot by the driving water, and a racing whirlpool gulps her down into the sea.
sentences.n: 'ast' is an old form of 'at', 'but', kept in epic for its archaic ring. 'illam' — the ship. 'ter' — 'three times', the usual number of epic repetition. 'torquet agens circum' — 'twists her, driving her round'. 'vortex' — whirlpool, from 'vorto', the old spelling of 'verto' (turn); later texts sometimes print 'vertex'. 'aequore' — ablative of place, 'in the sea'. The line ends on the whirlpool, as the ship does.

sentences.t:
Adparent rari nantes in gurgite vasto,
arma virum, tabulaeque, et Troia gaza per undas.
sentences.l:
There appear, scattered, men swimming in the vast abyss,
arms of men, and planks, and Trojan treasure across the waves.
sentences.i: A few men swim, scattered across the vast flood; on the waves float warriors' arms, ship's timbers, the treasure of Troy.
sentences.n: 'Adparent' is Greenough's spelling of 'apparent': he keeps the prefix unassimilated (ad-, not ap-). 'rari' — few and far between. 'gurgite' — properly a whirlpool or abyss, here the open sea. 'arma virum' — 'arms of men', with 'virum' the old genitive plural again — and an echo of the poem's first words, 'arma virumque': war and the man are going down together. 'gaza' is a Persian word for royal treasure, borrowed into Greek and Latin: a touch of eastern wealth for Troy.

sentences.i: Ilioneus' sturdy ship, brave Achates', the one that carried Abas and the one that bore old Aletes — one after another the storm has beaten them;
sentences.n: The roll-call of captains, held over two lines before the verb, tolls the losses one by one: 'iam… iam' ('now… now'), 'et qua… et qua'. 'Ilionei' is the genitive of Ilioneus, the -ei run together into one syllable (synizesis); 'Achati' is the genitive of Achates, a Greek name in -es declined as Latin. 'qua (navi) vectus (est)' — 'in which Abas was carried'; the verb is left out, and left out again with Aletes. 'hiems' — 'winter', regularly 'storm' in verse. 'grandaevus' — of great age.

sentences.t:
laxis laterum compagibus omnes
accipiunt inimicum imbrem, rimisque fatiscunt.
sentences.l:
with loosened joints of their sides, all
take in the hostile water, and with cracks they gape.
sentences.i: with the seams of their hulls sprung, all of them take in the enemy water and split open at every crack.
sentences.n: 'laxis laterum compagibus' — ablative absolute, 'the joinings of their sides having been loosened'. 'imbrem' — properly rain; here seawater, pouring in like a downpour. 'inimicum' — hostile: the water boards the ships like an enemy. 'rimis' — 'with cracks', ablative of means; 'fatiscunt' — gape, come apart. Read 'inimicum imbrem' with elision, 'inimic' imbrem'.

sentences.i: Meanwhile Neptune felt the sea heaving in a great roar, felt the storm unleashed and the calm of the deep floor stirred up from below, and was gravely troubled;
sentences.n: A long accusative and infinitive, all hanging on 'sensit': 'pontum misceri' (that the sea was being thrown into confusion), 'hiemem emissam (esse)' (that the storm had been let loose), 'stagna refusa (esse)' (that the still waters had been poured back). 'magno… murmure' — the m's rumble through the line. 'stagna' are the motionless waters of the sea-bed, the god's own domain, stirred now from 'imis vadis', the lowest depths. Neptune is Homer's Poseidon, but turned round: in Odyssey 5 Poseidon raises the storm against the hero; here the sea-god ends a storm he did not send. 'graviter commotus' — deeply stirred, angry.

sentences.t:
et alto
prospiciens, summa placidum caput extulit unda.
sentences.l:
and over the deep
looking out, from the top of the wave his calm head he raised.
sentences.i: and looking out across the open sea he raised his untroubled head from the top of the waves.
sentences.n: 'alto' — over the deep, the open sea. 'placidum' sits in pointed tension with 'graviter commotus' just before: angry within, the god shows the sea a calm face, and his calm is already the calm he will give the water. The point is a ruler's self-command. 'summa… unda' — 'from the top of the wave', ablative of the place from which.

sentences.t:
Disiectam Aeneae, toto videt aequore classem,
fluctibus oppressos Troas caelique ruina,
nec latuere doli fratrem Iunonis et irae.
sentences.i: There is Aeneas's fleet, strewn across the whole sea, the Trojans crushed by the waves and the collapsing sky; and her brother saw through Juno's tricks and Juno's rage.
sentences.n: 'Disiectam… classem' frames the line, the broken fleet spread across it (Greenough prints a comma after 'Aeneae'). 'Troas' is a Greek accusative plural (Tros, 'a Trojan'), with short -as. 'caeli ruina' — 'the collapse of the sky', the cloudburst, as if heaven were falling in. 'latuere' = 'latuerunt' (the -ere ending again); 'latere' with an accusative of the person means 'to escape someone's notice', and 'fratrem' is the one not deceived. Neptune and Juno are both children of Saturn: he knows his sister's ways. 'irae' — plural again, her resentments, as in line 11.

sentences.t: Eurum ad se Zephyrumque vocat, dehinc talia fatur:
sentences.l: Eurus to him and Zephyrus he calls, then such words speaks:
sentences.i: He summons the East Wind and the West, and then addresses them in these words:
sentences.n: Eurus (east) and Zephyrus (west) stand for all the winds. 'dehinc' — 'then', scanned as one syllable (synizesis). 'talia fatur' — 'speaks such things', a formula that introduces a speech, here running from the next line.

sentences.t: “Tantane vos generis tenuit fiducia vestri?
sentences.l: “Has such great trust in your lineage held you?
sentences.i: “Has pride in your ancestry so taken hold of you?
sentences.n: Neptune opens with indignant questions; '-ne' on 'Tanta' marks the question. 'generis vestri' — 'in your race': in Hesiod's Theogony the winds are sons of the Titan Astraeus and the Dawn, a Titan brood with Titan arrogance. The speech is short and sharp, a magistrate's rebuke rather than a god's tirade.

sentences.t:
Iam caelum terramque meo sine numine, venti,
miscere, et tantas audetis tollere moles?
sentences.l:
Now heaven and earth without my divine will, winds,
to throw into confusion, and such masses do you dare to raise?
sentences.i: Have you come to this, winds — daring to mix heaven and earth together without my leave, and heave up such mountains of water?
sentences.n: 'Iam' — 'now actually', indignant: you have come to this. 'meo sine numine' — the preposition between adjective and noun, a common verse order; 'numen' here is divine will and authority — without Neptune's consent, and in his own realm. Both infinitives hang on 'audetis'. 'moles' — masses, the mountainous waves. 'caelum terramque miscere' is exactly what Aeolus's restraint was there to prevent (lines 58–59).

sentences.t: Quos ego—sed motos praestat componere fluctus.
sentences.l: Whom I — but it is better the stirred-up waves to settle.
sentences.i: You whom I — But it is better first to settle the waves you have stirred.
sentences.n: The most famous break-off in Latin poetry, the figure rhetoricians call aposiopesis ('falling silent'): the threat — 'quos ego… (you) whom I (will punish)…' — is left unspoken, and the unsaid verb weighs more than any said one. Neptune masters himself in mid-sentence, and that self-mastery is the point of the scene. 'Quos ego' became proverbial for a threat held back. 'quos' — 'whom', a relative whose antecedent is the 'vos' (you winds) of his opening question. 'praestat' — impersonal, 'it is better', with the infinitive 'componere'. 'componere' — to put together, settle, set in order: Neptune turns from punishment to restoring calm, the business at hand. 'motos… fluctus' frames the clause.

sentences.t: Post mihi non simili poena commissa luetis.
sentences.l: Later to me with no like penalty your offences you will pay for.
sentences.i: Another time you will pay me for your crimes with no such light penalty.
sentences.n: 'Post' — afterwards, another time. 'mihi' — dative, 'to me', the one owed the penalty. 'non simili poena' — 'with no similar penalty', understatement (litotes): with a far heavier one than this rebuke. 'commissa' — 'things committed', offences, a neuter plural participle used as a noun. 'luo' — pay, atone for.

sentences.t: Maturate fugam, regique haec dicite vestro:
sentences.l: Hasten your flight, and to your king these words say:
sentences.i: Be off at once, and give your king this message:
sentences.n: 'Maturate fugam' — 'speed up your flight', a brusque dismissal. 'regi vestro' — 'your king' is Aeolus, and the 'your' is contemptuous: king of you, and of nothing more. The colon opens the message itself.

sentences.t:
non illi imperium pelagi saevumque tridentem,
sed mihi sorte datum.
sentences.l:
not to him the rule of the sea and the fierce trident,
but to me by lot was given.
sentences.i: the sea's empire and the fierce trident fell by lot not to him but to me.
sentences.n: 'illi… mihi' — 'to him… to me', datives set against each other at the heads of their clauses. 'sorte' — 'by lot': after the fall of Saturn his three sons drew lots for sky, sea and underworld, as Poseidon recalls in Iliad 15. 'datum (est)' is neuter, agreeing with 'imperium', the first and weightier noun — or with the pair taken as one thing. 'tridentem' — the trident, the three-pronged spear that is the sea-god's sceptre.

sentences.t:
Tenet ille immania saxa,
vestras, Eure, domos;
sentences.l:
He holds huge rocks,
your homes, Eurus;
sentences.i: His domain is the monstrous crags — your homes, East Wind;
sentences.n: 'ille' — 'that one', Aeolus, said with contempt. 'vestras… domos' stands in apposition to 'saxa': the rocks are your houses. Neptune names Eurus ('Eure', vocative) but means all the winds — 'vestras' is plural. The rocks are the cave-prison of lines 52–54.

sentences.t:
illa se iactet in aula
Aeolus, et clauso ventorum carcere regnet.”
sentences.l:
in that hall let him swagger,
Aeolus, and, the prison of the winds shut, let him reign.”
sentences.i: let Aeolus strut in that hall of his, and be king there — with the winds' prison shut.”
sentences.n: 'iactet' and 'regnet' are jussive subjunctives, 'let him…'. 'se iactare' — to toss oneself about, to show off. 'illa… aula' — 'that court of his', contemptuous again. 'clauso… carcere' — ablative absolute, 'the prison having been shut': Aeolus may reign only while the doors stay closed, a pointed reply to his letting the winds out at lines 81–83. The speech ends here, with Greenough's closing mark.

sentences.t:
Sic ait, et dicto citius tumida aequora placat,
collectasque fugat nubes, solemque reducit.
sentences.l:
So he speaks, and quicker than the word the swollen seas he calms,
and the gathered clouds puts to flight, and the sun brings back.
sentences.i: With these words — and before the words were done — he levels the swelling seas, scatters the banked clouds and brings back the sun.
sentences.n: 'Sic ait' — 'so he speaks', the formula that closes a speech, as 'talia fatur' opened it. 'dicto citius' — 'quicker than the word', ablative of comparison: the calm comes before the speech is done. The three verbs, 'placat… fugat… reducit', each closing its clause, make an orderly sequence where the storm was chaos. 'tumida aequora' is elided, 'tumid' aequora'.

sentences.t:
Cymothoe simul et Triton adnixus acuto
detrudunt navis scopulo;
sentences.l:
Cymothoe together with Triton, straining, from the sharp
rock push off the ships;
sentences.i: Cymothoe and Triton, heaving together, shove the ships off the jagged rock;
sentences.n: Cymothoe is a Nereid, one of the sea-nymphs, daughters of Nereus; Triton is Neptune's son, a merman, the sea's trumpeter. 'adnixus' (from 'adnitor', Greenough's unassimilated spelling of 'annixus') — 'leaning hard against', putting his shoulder to it. 'acuto… scopulo' — ablative of separation, 'from the sharp rock', split across the line-end. 'navis' is the -is accusative plural. The plural verb follows the two subjects joined by 'simul et'.

sentences.t: levat ipse tridenti;
sentences.l: he himself lifts with his trident;
sentences.i: the god himself prises them up with his trident;
sentences.n: 'ipse' — Neptune himself, as against his helpers. 'tridenti' is ablative, with the i-stem ending -i: 'with the trident'. The god levers the stranded ships free.

sentences.t:
et vastas aperit syrtis, et temperat aequor,
atque rotis summas levibus perlabitur undas.
sentences.l:
and he opens the vast sandbanks, and tempers the sea,
and on light wheels he glides over the tops of the waves.
sentences.i: He clears a way through the vast sandbanks, soothes the sea, and skims on light wheels over the surface of the waves.
sentences.n: 'syrtis' here is a common noun, any sandbank (compare the Syrtes of line 111), in the -is accusative plural. 'aperit' — clears a passage through them. 'temperat' is the word used of Aeolus calming the winds (line 57). 'rotis… levibus' wraps round 'summas', and 'summas… undas' round the verb. The sea-god driving his chariot over the waves comes from Iliad 13, where Poseidon's horses carry him across the sea and the sea-creatures come up to greet their lord.

sentences.i: And as so often happens in a great nation, when a riot has broken out and the lowborn mob runs wild with passion, and already torches and stones are flying — their frenzy arms them with whatever lies to hand —
sentences.n: The poem's first full-scale simile, and a startling one. Homer compares crowds to the sea (Iliad 2, the assembly heaving like waves); Virgil turns it round and compares the sea to a crowd, explaining nature by Roman politics. 'Ac veluti… cum' — 'and just as when…', answered by 'sic' in line 154. 'coorta est' — 'has arisen', a thing that happens time and again ('saepe'). 'volgus' is Greenough's spelling of 'vulgus', the older vowel, as in 'volnus' for 'vulnus'. 'animis' — 'in their spirits', ablative of respect. 'furor arma ministrat' — 'rage hands out the weapons', whatever lies to hand: a much-quoted half-line. A Roman reader would think of the street riots of the late Republic.

sentences.t:
tum, pietate gravem ac meritis si forte virum quem
conspexere, silent, arrectisque auribus adstant;
sentences.l:
then, weighty in devotion and services, if by chance some man
they have caught sight of, they fall silent, and with ears pricked they stand by;
sentences.i: then, if they chance to catch sight of some man whose devotion and services give him weight, they fall silent and stand still with ears alert;
sentences.n: 'pietate gravem ac meritis' — 'weighty with devotion and services': 'gravis' is the Roman virtue of 'gravitas', moral weight and authority; 'pietas' is Aeneas's own virtue (line 10). 'si… quem' — after 'si', 'quis/qui' means 'some, any' ('quem' = 'aliquem'); you'll see this again. 'conspexere' = 'conspexerunt'. 'arrectis auribus' — ablative absolute, 'with ears pricked up', a picture from animals listening. 'adstant' — Greenough's unassimilated spelling of 'astant'. The man is left unnamed: Virgil keeps him a type.

sentences.t:
ille regit dictis animos, et pectora mulcet,—
sic cunctus pelagi cecidit fragor, aequora postquam
prospiciens genitor caeloque invectus aperto
flectit equos, curruque volans dat lora secundo.
sentences.l:
he rules with words their spirits, and their hearts soothes —
so all the crashing of the sea fell, once, over the waters
looking out, the father, and borne along under open sky,
turns his horses, and flying gives rein to his willing chariot.
sentences.i: and he governs their passions with his words and calms their hearts — so all the uproar of the sea died away, once the father, gazing out over the waters and riding under a sky now clear, wheeled his horses and, flying, gave free rein to his easy-running chariot.
sentences.n: 'ille' — the man of weight; words ('dictis') are his only weapon against the mob's stones. 'mulcet' — strokes, soothes: Aeneas will do the same for his men at line 197. 'sic' answers 'veluti' (148) and brings us back to the sea. 'cecidit fragor' — 'the crashing fell', died down. 'aequora postquam' — 'postquam' placed after a word of its own clause, common in verse. 'genitor' — 'the father', a title of honour for a great god, here Neptune. 'caelo aperto' — under a sky now opened, cleared. 'curru… secundo' — the chariot 'following', running easily behind the horses; 'dat lora' — 'gives the reins', lets the horses run.

sentences.t:
Defessi Aeneadae, quae proxima litora, cursu
contendunt petere, et Libyae vertuntur ad oras.
sentences.l:
Worn out, the men of Aeneas, the shores which are nearest, by sailing
strive to reach, and toward Libya's coasts are turned.
sentences.i: Aeneas's weary men strain to reach whatever shore lies nearest, and turn toward the coasts of Libya.
sentences.n: 'Aeneadae' — 'sons of Aeneas', a patronymic used of his followers; Lucretius' poem opens 'Aeneadum genetrix', mother of the Aeneadae, meaning the Romans, who saw themselves as Aeneas's people. 'quae proxima litora' — 'the shores which (are) nearest': the antecedent is drawn into the relative clause, so 'they strive to reach the nearest shores'. 'cursu' — 'in their course', by sailing. 'vertuntur' — middle in sense, 'they turn themselves'. Libya is the Roman name for North Africa in general; they will land not far from Carthage.

sentences.t: Est in secessu longo locus:
sentences.l: There is in a long recess a place:
sentences.i: Far up a long bay there is a place:
sentences.n: 'Est… locus' — 'there is a place', the standard opening of a set description (an ecphrasis): the story pauses to paint a scene, and you will meet 'est locus' again. 'secessu longo' — a long withdrawal of the coast, a deep inlet. The harbour is modelled on two in the Odyssey: the harbour by the Cyclopes' land in Book 9 and the harbour of Phorcys on Ithaca, with its cave of the nymphs, in Book 13. No real harbour need be looked for.

sentences.t:
insula portum
efficit obiectu laterum, quibus omnis ab alto
frangitur inque sinus scindit sese unda reductos.
sentences.l:
an island a harbour
makes by the obstruction of its flanks, against which every wave from the deep
is broken, and into withdrawn bays splits itself.
sentences.i: an island lying across its mouth makes a harbour: its flanks are a screen where every swell from the open sea shatters and divides into the deep-set bays.
sentences.n: 'obiectu laterum' — 'by the throwing-across of its sides': the island lies across the mouth of the inlet, and its flanks shelter the water. 'quibus' — 'on (against) which', the island's sides. 'omnis… unda' — 'every wave', subject and adjective far apart, the wave travelling the length of the line. 'inque sinus… reductos' — 'and into withdrawn bays', 'reductus' meaning set back. 'scindit sese' — splits itself. 'omnis' here is nominative singular.

sentences.i: Huge cliffs rise menacing on either side, twin crags threatening the sky, and under their summits the water lies safe and silent over a wide expanse;
sentences.n: 'Hinc atque hinc' — 'from here and from here', on both sides. 'minantur in caelum' — 'threaten into the sky', rise steep and menacing. 'gemini… scopuli' — 'twin crags', split across the line-end. 'quorum sub vertice' — 'beneath whose peak'. 'aequora tuta silent' — 'the safe waters are silent', stillness after the storm's noise; 'silent' is the word of the hushed crowd in the simile (152).

sentences.t:
tum silvis scaena coruscis
desuper horrentique atrum nemus imminet umbra.
sentences.l:
then with quivering woods a backdrop
from above, and a black grove overhangs with bristling shade.
sentences.i: above them rises a backdrop of shimmering woods, and a dark grove looms overhead in its shaggy shade.
sentences.n: 'scaena' (Greenough's spelling; also 'scena') is a theatre word, the stage's painted back wall: the woods rise behind the harbour like a stage-set, and the reader sits in the audience. 'coruscis' — quivering, flickering with light. 'horrenti… umbra' — 'with bristling shade', the trees standing up like hair on end ('horreo'). 'atrum nemus' — a black grove; a 'nemus' is often a sacred wood. The verb of the first clause ('est') is understood. 'horrentique atrum' is elided, 'horrentiqu' atrum'.

sentences.t:
Fronte sub adversa scopulis pendentibus antrum,
intus aquae dulces vivoque sedilia saxo,
nympharum domus:
sentences.i: Under the cliff-face opposite is a cave of overhanging rock, with fresh water inside and seats of natural stone — a dwelling of the nymphs;
sentences.n: No verb at all: a list, as in an inventory. 'Fronte sub adversa' — 'under the facing front', the cliff that fronts the harbour mouth. 'scopulis pendentibus' — 'of hanging rocks', ablative of description. 'aquae dulces' — 'sweet waters', fresh water, a sailor's first need. 'vivo… saxo' — 'living rock', stone left as it grew, not quarried. The cave of the nymphs comes from the harbour of Phorcys in Odyssey 13, where Odysseus is set ashore asleep on Ithaca.

sentences.t:
hic fessas non vincula navis
ulla tenent, unco non alligat ancora morsu.
sentences.l:
here weary ships no cables
at all hold, no anchor ties them with its hooked bite.
sentences.i: here no mooring-ropes are needed to hold the weary ships, no anchor to grip them with its hooked tooth.
sentences.n: 'fessas… navis' — the ships themselves are weary, like their crews; 'navis' is the -is accusative plural. 'non… ulla' — 'not any', emphatic. 'unco… morsu' — 'with its hooked bite', the anchor's fluke biting the sea-floor. Homer says the same of the harbour in Odyssey 9: no need there of cables or anchor-stones.

sentences.t:
Huc septem Aeneas collectis navibus omni
ex numero subit;
sentences.l:
To this place, with seven ships gathered from the whole
number, Aeneas enters;
sentences.i: Into this haven Aeneas comes with seven ships gathered from all his fleet;
sentences.n: 'Huc' — 'to here', motion towards. 'septem… collectis navibus' — ablative absolute, 'seven ships having been gathered', which English says as 'with seven ships'. 'omni ex numero' — 'out of the whole number': he sailed with twenty, as he tells his mother at line 381, so thirteen are missing — one of them, Orontes' ship, sunk before his eyes; the rest will come back into the story later in the book. 'subit' — goes in, enters the harbour.

sentences.t:
ac magno telluris amore
egressi optata potiuntur Troes harena,
et sale tabentis artus in litore ponunt.
sentences.l:
and with a great love of the land,
having landed, of the longed-for sand the Trojans take possession,
and their limbs, soaked with brine, on the shore they lay down.
sentences.i: and the Trojans, aching for solid ground, climb out, take possession of the sand they had prayed for, and lay their salt-sodden bodies down on the shore.
sentences.n: 'telluris amore' — 'with love of the land', an objective genitive: they long for the land. 'egressi' — 'having gone out', disembarked. 'potiuntur' takes the ablative: 'they make themselves masters of the longed-for sand'. 'Troes' is the Greek nominative plural of 'Tros', a Trojan. 'tabentis' — 'dripping, wasting', the -is accusative plural agreeing with 'artus'. 'sale' — 'with salt', the sea.

sentences.t:
Ac primum silici scintillam excudit Achates,
succepitque ignem foliis, atque arida circum
nutrimenta dedit, rapuitque in fomite flammam.
sentences.l:
And first from flint a spark struck out Achates,
and caught the fire in leaves, and dry around it
fuel gave, and snatched up in the tinder the flame.
sentences.i: First Achates strikes flint and draws a spark, lets the leaves take it, feeds it with dry fuel heaped round, and soon has a flame leaping in the tinder.
sentences.n: 'silici' — 'from the flint', a dative with a verb of taking away. 'excudit' — perfect, 'struck out' (the u is long here, ex-cū-dit, as the metre shows; the present would have a short u), like 'succepit', 'dedit', 'rapuit': a quick series of completed acts. 'succepit' is Greenough's spelling of 'suscepit', 'caught it (from beneath)'. 'nutrimenta' — food for the fire. 'rapuit in fomite flammam' — 'seized the flame in the tinder', made it catch at once. Fire-making, the first act ashore, is told in close detail, a Homeric attention to ordinary work; compare the end of Odyssey 5, where shipwrecked Odysseus buries himself in leaves like an ember banked to keep a fire alive.

sentences.t:
Tum Cererem corruptam undis Cerealiaque arma
expediunt fessi rerum, frugesque receptas
et torrere parant flammis et frangere saxo.
sentences.l:
Then Ceres spoiled by the waves and Ceres' weapons
they bring out, weary of their fortunes, and the grain recovered
both to parch they prepare with flames and to crush with stone.
sentences.i: Then, worn out by their troubles, they bring out the sea-soaked grain and the tools for making bread, and set about parching the salvaged corn over the fire and grinding it with stone.
sentences.n: 'Cererem' — Ceres, goddess of grain, for the grain itself (metonymy, a god's name for what the god governs, as 'Bacchus' for wine). 'Cerealia arma' — 'the weapons of Ceres', a mock-heroic name for the kitchen gear: mills, troughs, sieves. 'Cerealiaque arma' is elided, 'Cerealiaqu' arma'. 'fessi rerum' — 'weary of things', of their troubles; a genitive with an adjective. 'fruges receptas' — the grain saved from the wreck. 'et… et' — 'both… and': grain was parched before it was ground.

sentences.t:
Aeneas scopulum interea conscendit, et omnem
prospectum late pelago petit, Anthea si quem
iactatum vento videat Phrygiasque biremis,
aut Capyn, aut celsis in puppibus arma Caici.
sentences.l:
Aeneas a crag meanwhile climbs, and the whole
view far and wide over the sea seeks, if any Antheus
tossed by the wind he might see, and the Phrygian biremes,
or Capys, or on high sterns the arms of Caicus.
sentences.i: Meanwhile Aeneas climbs a crag and sweeps the whole broad sea with his eyes, hoping to sight Antheus driven by the gale, or the Phrygian galleys, or Capys, or Caicus's shields hung high on a stern.
sentences.n: 'interea' — meanwhile, while the men cook. 'omnem prospectum… petit' — 'seeks the whole view', scans the whole sea. 'Anthea si quem… videat' — 'if he might see any Antheus', Antheus or anyone at all; 'si quem' again = 'si aliquem', and the subjunctive 'videat' gives the hope behind his looking. 'Anthea' (Antheus) and 'Capyn' (Capys) are Greek accusatives; 'Caici' is genitive. 'Phrygias' — Trojan (Phrygia was the region round Troy). 'biremis' — biremes, ships with two banks of oars, in the -is accusative plural. 'arma… in puppibus' — shields hung on the high sterns, marking a captain's ship. The look-out from a height followed by a stag-hunt comes from Odysseus on Circe's island, Odyssey 10.

sentences.t:
Navem in conspectu nullam, tris litore cervos
prospicit errantis;
sentences.l:
A ship in sight, none; three on the shore stags
he spies wandering;
sentences.i: Not a ship to be seen; but on the shore he spots three stags wandering;
sentences.n: 'Navem… nullam' — 'no ship', the adjective held back for the bad news. No 'but' joins the two clauses (asyndeton): disappointment and the new sight stand side by side. 'tris… errantis' — -is accusative plurals again, agreeing with 'cervos'. 'litore' — ablative of place, 'on the shore'.

sentences.t:
hos tota armenta sequuntur
a tergo, et longum per vallis pascitur agmen.
sentences.l:
these whole herds follow
from behind, and through the valleys a long column grazes.
sentences.i: behind them trails the entire herd, a long column grazing down the valleys.
sentences.n: 'armenta' — properly herds of cattle, here of deer. 'a tergo' — 'from the back', behind. 'agmen' is a military word, an army column on the march: the deer are described as an army, with leaders and rank and file to come. 'vallis' — -is accusative plural after 'per'.

sentences.t:
Constitit hic, arcumque manu celerisque sagittas
corripuit, fidus quae tela gerebat Achates;
sentences.l:
He halted here, and the bow in hand and the swift arrows
snatched up, which weapons loyal Achates bore;
sentences.i: He stopped where he was and caught up the bow and the fleet arrows that loyal Achates bore for him;
sentences.n: 'Constitit hic' — 'he stood still here', the hunter's pause. 'celeris' — -is accusative plural with 'sagittas'. 'quae tela' — 'which weapons': the antecedent (bow and arrows) restated inside the relative clause as 'tela'. 'fidus Achates' — 'faithful Achates', his standing epithet; the pair becomes a fixed formula through the poem, as Homer's heroes have theirs. Achates carries his weapons here: he is Aeneas's constant companion.

sentences.i: first he brings down the leaders, heads held high under antlers like branching trees, then the common herd, and his arrows drive the whole mob in confusion through the leafy woods;
sentences.n: The hunt is told in the language of war and politics: 'ductores' (generals), 'volgus' (the common people, the word of the riot simile, line 149), 'turbam' (the mob). 'ferentis' — -is accusative plural, agreeing with 'ductores'. 'cornibus arboreis' — 'tree-like horns', branching antlers. 'sternit' — 'strews', lays low. 'nemora inter frondea' — the preposition after its first word (anastrophe), common in verse. 'miscet agens' — 'drives and throws into confusion'.

sentences.t:
nec prius absistit, quam septem ingentia victor
corpora fundat humi, et numerum cum navibus aequet.
sentences.l:
nor sooner does he stop than seven huge, as victor,
bodies he lays on the ground, and the number with the ships makes equal.
sentences.i: and he does not stop until, victorious, he has laid seven great carcasses on the earth, one for each ship.
sentences.n: 'prius… quam' — 'before, until', split in two (tmesis of 'priusquam'); with the subjunctive ('fundat', 'aequet') it looks ahead to an aim. 'humi' — locative, 'on the ground'. 'victor' — 'as victor', a battlefield word again. 'numerum cum navibus aequet' — 'makes the number equal with the ships': a deer for each of the seven crews. In Odyssey 10 Odysseus kills one great stag for his men; Virgil's hero kills seven.

sentences.t: Hinc portum petit, et socios partitur in omnes.
sentences.l: From there the harbour he seeks, and among his comrades shares them out, all.
sentences.i: Then he makes for the harbour and divides the meat among all his comrades.
sentences.n: 'Hinc' — from here (and so, next). 'partitur' — deponent, 'divides, shares out'; the object, the deer, is understood. 'socios… in omnes' — 'among all his comrades', with 'omnes' at the line-end: no one is left out. Sharing the spoils fairly is a leader's duty.

sentences.t:
Vina bonus quae deinde cadis onerarat Acestes
litore Trinacrio dederatque abeuntibus heros,
dividit, et dictis maerentia pectora mulcet:
sentences.l:
Next, the wine which kindly Acestes had stowed in jars
on the Trinacrian shore and, hero that he was, given them as they left,
he shares out, and with words their grieving hearts he soothes:
sentences.i: Next he shares out the wine that good Acestes, like the prince he was, had loaded into jars on the Sicilian shore and given them as they sailed, and he soothes their grieving hearts with these words:
sentences.n: 'deinde' belongs with 'dividit' — 'next he shares out' — though it stands inside the relative clause; the antecedent 'vina' comes first, the relative 'quae' after it. 'bonus… Acestes' — 'kind Acestes', the adjective a line's length from its noun. Acestes is a Sicilian king of Trojan descent, who had given them hospitality on the island; Book 5 returns to him. 'onerarat' = 'oneraverat', a shortened (syncopated) pluperfect, 'had loaded'; 'cadis' — 'in jars'. 'Trinacrio' — Sicilian: Trinacria, 'the three-cornered', is a Greek name for Sicily. 'heros' — 'the hero', a title of honour for Acestes. 'pectora mulcet' repeats the words of the statesman in the simile (153): Aeneas calms his men as Neptune calmed the sea. The colon opens his speech, which begins the next part.
